1.explanation:
· link.config.js drives the CSS token output for the Link component and needs to be extended to emit the new `--inline` modifier rules (text-decoration: underline, color tokens per state).
· Link.js is the React component that needs to add the `inline` prop to its className logic so that when inline={true} it adds `${prefix}--link--inline`.
· Link-test.js must include unit tests for the inline variant (ensuring the inline CSS class is present and the right style props flow through).
· Link-story.js should demonstrate the new inline link variant in Storybook so designers and devs can review the visual treatment across all states.
1.bug_scenario: The spec artboards show a new “inline link” variant for the Link component that should be underlined by default (with specific type tokens and text‐decoration) and then change color/underline per state (hover, active, focus, disabled, visited) across light and dark backgrounds. In our Storybook and in production the <Link inline> prop currently does not produce the underlined style or correct CSS class and states.

2.explanation:
• link.config.js – this is where we register the ‘inline’ modifier and define the class name conventions for our web-component version of Link; if the inline style isn’t wired up correctly here, the SCSS compiler won’t emit the proper CSS rules.

• link.scss – this SCSS file must contain the “.bx--link--inline { text-decoration: underline; }” rule plus all of the pseudo-state rules (hover, active, focus, disabled, visited). Those rules are missing or incomplete, so the inline link never gets underlined or changes color as specified.

• Link.js – the React wrapper needs to ensure that passing inline={true} adds the inline modifier class by default, and that disabling still preserves the underline (or applies the correct css class). If the component logic drops the underline class or mis-names it, you’ll see no underline at runtime.

• Link-test.js – the unit tests currently only check for the presence of the base link class and the inline modifier, but they don’t assert that the CSS classes are applied consistently across states. We’ll need to update or add tests to verify that inline links always carry the underline class and that the disabled/visited/hover modifiers are present.

• Link-story.js – the Storybook example for Link should demonstrate the new inline behavior (including underlines in all states). We’ll update the story to show a paragraph of inline text links with underlines so reviewers can visually confirm the change.

By updating these five files, we will wire up the inline variant in our style registry, author the missing CSS rules, ensure the React API honors the new variant, and add visual tests/examples to lock in the expected behavior.
2.bug_scenario: The spec for “inline” links requires that by default any <Link inline> should render with an underline, and that underline should persist across disabled, hover, active, focus, and visited states—only the color (or outline) should change. In the screenshot you can see the desired behaviors: underlined text in the default state, color blue on hover, darker text when active, a 1px outline on focus, gray text on disabled, and purple on visited. In our repro, however, the inline variant is either rendering without any underline, or the CSS rules for the pseudo-states (hover/active/focus/visited/disabled) are missing or incomplete.
